attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, in his own authorial voice. This is not a quotation of Saunders.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' with an explicit antecedent (succeed in torpedoing SB-1047). It keeps the 'in many ways' scope and treats slow federal action as an explanatory qualifier. No deadline is stated.

contract.note: Requiring that the opponents' efforts contributed causally fits the ordinary reading of 'succeed in torpedoing'. Reading 'in many ways' as substantial reliance on voluntary company choices is ordinary and not stretched either way. The result still turns on these readings, because the speaker named no measure.

evidence.note: Official veto message. It establishes that the bill was defeated, but not that OpenAI or others caused the defeat. It bears on the antecedent, not on the predicted outcome.
CalMatters names OpenAI, Google and Meta as opponents. This shows opposition only, not causal influence on the veto, so it does not settle the antecedent.

SB 53 (2025) imposes enforceable disclosure, incident reporting and penalties. This is relevant to how much remains voluntary, but it is not decisive under the qualified 'in many ways', and the antecedent is unestablished.

reviews.rationale: The veto and the industry opposition are documented, but the packet does not establish that OpenAI and others contributed causally to the defeat. The contract requires that. With the antecedent unknown, the forecast cannot be scored. SB 53's binding obligations are material context, but they do not decisively displace reliance on voluntary choices. No early-resolution event is met and no deadline was stated.
